verses.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Go in to Pharaoh, and tell him, ‘This is what Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews, says: “Let my people go, that they may serve me.
For if you refuse to let them go, and hold them still,
behold, Yahweh’s hand is on your livestock which are in the field, on the horses, on the donkeys, on the camels, on the herds, and on the flocks with a very grievous pestilence.
Yahweh will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt; and nothing shall die of all that belongs to the children of Israel.”’”
Yahweh appointed a set time, saying, “Tomorrow Yahweh shall do this thing in the land.”
Yahweh did that thing on the next day; and all the livestock of Egypt died, but of the livestock of the children of Israel, not one died.
Pharaoh sent, and, behold, there was not so much as one of the livestock of the Israelites dead. But the heart of Pharaoh was stubborn, and he didn’t let the people go.
Yahweh said to Moses and to Aaron, “Take to you handfuls of ashes of the furnace, and let Moses sprinkle it toward the sky in the sight of Pharaoh.
It shall become small dust over all the land of Egypt, and shall be a boil breaking out with boils on man and on animal, throughout all the land of Egypt.”
They took ashes of the furnace, and stood before Pharaoh; and Moses sprinkled it up toward the sky; and it became a boil breaking out with boils on man and on animal.
The magicians couldn’t stand before Moses because of the boils; for the boils were on the magicians, and on all the Egyptians.
Yahweh hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he didn’t listen to them, as Yahweh had spoken to Moses.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Rise up early in the morning, and stand before Pharaoh, and tell him, ‘This is what Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews, says: “Let my people go, that they may serve me.
For this time I will send all my plagues against your heart, against your officials, and against your people; that you may know that there is no one like me in all the earth.
For now I would have stretched out my hand, and struck you and your people with pestilence, and you would have been cut off from the earth;
but indeed for this cause I have made you stand: to show you my power, and that my name may be declared throughout all the earth;
as you still exalt yourself against my people, that you won’t let them go.
Behold, tomorrow about this time I will cause it to rain a very grievous hail, such as has not been in Egypt since the day it was founded even until now.

Now therefore command that all of your livestock and all that you have in the field be brought into shelter. Every man and animal that is found in the field, and isn’t brought home, the hail shall come down on them, and they shall die.”’”
Those who feared Yahweh’s word among the servants of Pharaoh made their servants and their livestock flee into the houses.
Whoever didn’t respect Yahweh’s word left his servants and his livestock in the field.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward the sky, that there may be hail in all the land of Egypt, on man, and on animal, and on every herb of the field, throughout the land of Egypt.”
Moses stretched out his rod toward the heavens, and Yahweh sent thunder, hail, and lightning flashed down to the earth. Yahweh rained hail on the land of Egypt.
So there was very severe hail, and lightning mixed with the hail, such as had not been in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation.
The hail struck throughout all the land of Egypt all that was in the field, both man and animal; and the hail struck every herb of the field, and broke every tree of the field.
Only in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, there was no hail.
Pharaoh sent, and called for Moses and Aaron, and said to them, “I have sinned this time. Yahweh is righteous, and I and my people are wicked.
Pray to Yahweh; for there has been enough of mighty thunderings and hail. I will let you go, and you shall stay no longer.”

Moses said to him, “As soon as I have gone out of the city, I will spread abroad my hands to Yahweh. The thunders shall cease, and there will not be any more hail; that you may know that the earth is Yahweh’s.
But as for you and your servants, I know that you don’t yet fear Yahweh God.”
The flax and the barley were struck, for the barley was in the ear, and the flax was in bloom.
But the wheat and the spelt were not struck, for they had not grown up.
Moses went out of the city from Pharaoh, and spread abroad his hands to Yahweh; and the thunders and hail ceased, and the rain was not poured on the earth.
When Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunders had ceased, he sinned yet more, and hardened his heart, he and his servants.
The heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he didn’t let the children of Israel go, just as Yahweh had spoken through Moses.

footnotes.content: Moses is sent again to Pharaoh with the same plea: 'Let my people go.' How many times must a man repeat himself before he is heard? Yet God sends Moses again, and again. There is a patience here that will not wear out—like our Lord coming to us, over and over, calling us toward freedom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The condition is laid bare: if you refuse, this thing will follow. Every refusal has a cost. I've learned that stubbornness always exacts a price, though we keep hoping it won't. The God of mercy speaks, but He speaks truly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh's hand touches the livestock—horses, camels, herds, flocks. What Egypt depends on for wealth and power becomes the instrument of its ruin. God strikes not vindictively but to show that He alone holds dominion over what men treasure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A distinction is made: Israel's herds will be spared. This is the heart of God's covenant work—to separate a people for Himself. Even in judgment, He guards those who are His. That distinction still stands for those who belong to Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh appointed a set time. Tomorrow. God does not act in chaos or shadow—He speaks plainly what He will do. There is something steadying in that clarity, even when judgment is coming. We can trust the God whose word is sure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: It happened as God said. All Egypt's livestock died, but Israel lost nothing. When we read this through the lens of the cross, we see the Substitute once more: one nation's loss became another's deliverance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh saw the truth—not one Israelite animal died—yet his heart remained stubborn. How often we see God work and still turn away. The hardness described here is not fate; it is choice, and choice has a weight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses takes ashes from the furnace and scatters them toward heaven. The furnace speaks of fire and refining; the ashes speak of judgment. All that is burned away becomes a sign. Even our ashes can become God's message to the world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The small dust becomes boils—tiny ashes turn to painful sores. God uses what is small and overlooked to humble the mighty. The Healer became wounded for us, taking boils of sin upon Himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What was spoken came to pass exactly. The word and the work are one. The magicians who once mimicked God's power are now helpless. There are limits to human knowledge and craft; only God's word carries true power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The magicians, who had stood before Moses in contest, now cannot stand. They too bear the boils. Pharaoh's advisors are brought low. Sometimes the Lord's way of making His point is to silence the counselors of pride.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not listen. This hardening is not the first; it mirrors what has come before. When a man continually refuses to hear, his ability to hear can be taken from him. The choice we make repeatedly becomes the soul we become.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rise up early. God's messenger stands before the king at dawn, with the same word on his lips. There is no wavering in Moses here, no exhaustion. When you serve the Living God, you can return to the hard place again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This time God will send all His plagues—against Pharaoh's heart, his officials, his people—that they may know He has no equal. The point is not destruction for its own sake; it is knowledge: that the God of the Hebrews is Lord of all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh could have struck Pharaoh and his people with pestilence and cut them off. But He did not. There is a mercy here underneath the judgment, a space given for repentance. Even in severity, God holds back His full hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh was raised up to show God's power and declare His name throughout the earth. Even the one who resists becomes an instrument of God's glory. Every stubborn heart, overcome by grace, testifies to what the Lord can do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Still Pharaoh exalts himself. Pride returns like a man who keeps opening the same wound. He will not let the people go. The rebellion is so deep that only judgment can break it—and even then, the heart may close again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tomorrow hail will fall—the worst Egypt has ever known. Warning precedes the blow. God tells before He strikes. Such tenderness in the severity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bring your servants and livestock into shelter. The Lord gives a way of escape. For those who hear and obey, refuge is prepared. But those who ignore the warning will find themselves exposed to the very judgment they were given time to avoid.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those who feared Yahweh's word made haste to obey. Fear of the Lord—not panic, but reverence for His truth—becomes the thing that saves. In every crisis, it is the reverent who escape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those who did not respect the word left everything in the field. The choice was clear; the way was given; they did not walk it. That refusal had a cost that came in the next verse.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses stretches out his hand toward the sky at God's command. What a thing to receive—to hold the rod that calls judgment down. Yet Moses acts in obedience, not in wrath. He is God's instrument.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thunder and hail and lightning—the heavens joined the work. Yahweh sent it. When God acts, all creation responds. The powers that Pharaoh thought to master now come down upon him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The hail was severe as never before. No one who lived in Egypt had seen judgment like this. It was a moment that shattered memory and expectation. Sometimes the Lord breaks through all that we have known.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The hail struck everything—man and animal and every herb and tree. Nothing was spared that had been left exposed. A complete judgment, total in its reach. This is what refusal looks like at the end of its course.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In Goshen, where Israel dwelt, there was no hail. A wall of protection. God's people stood untouched while the storm broke around them. This is the promise to all who belong to Him—safety in the shelter of His covenant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At last Pharaoh breaks. 'I have sinned. You are righteous; I and my people are wicked.' The admission comes after the judgment. He sees now what he refused to see before. Repentance, yes—but it comes late.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh asks Moses to pray the thunder to cease. He recognizes Moses' power with God and begs relief. 'I will let you go.' The words he has fought to withhold for so long. Judgment can break what stubbornness would not yield.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses will go out and spread his hands in prayer, and the thunders will cease. 'That you may know the earth is Yahweh's.' Even in granting relief, Moses points to the deeper truth. The earth belongs to God, not to any king.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But I know you do not yet fear Yahweh God. Moses speaks with clear sight. Pharaoh's confession is real, but it is not true fear. There is a difference between being frightened by judgment and fearing God. One can pass; the other transforms.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The flax and barley were struck—both in their ripeness. The crops ready for harvest were destroyed. What Egypt had cultivated and tended was taken in a moment. This speaks to the fragility of what we rely on without God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wheat and spelt had not grown up, so they were spared. Even in judgment, God's provision is mixed with mercy. Some crops remain. Even in ruin, there is seed for tomorrow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses goes out and spreads his hands, and the storm stops. The thunder ceases; the rain ends. The power of prayer in the hands of one who trusts God is real. Obedience and intercession can call down mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the hail stopped, Pharaoh sinned again and hardened his heart—he and his servants. The relief becomes a return to rebellion. Without a true turning to God, the moment of submission passes and the old resistance returns.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not let Israel go, as Yahweh had spoken. Looking back from the distance of years, I see how often the Lord spoke what would come to pass—not to predict a fate we cannot escape, but to say: I have seen, I know, and I will deliver My people despite all hardness. We can trust that word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
